name: Composition over inheritance
statement: Assemble behaviour from parts instead of inheriting it.

name: Law of Demeter, tell don't ask
statement: Talk to your neighbours, not to their internals.

caveat: Derivation needs somewhere to derive from: a table, a macro, a type. If building it costs more than the drift it prevents, a test over two copies is the honest fallback. Say so, and keep it small.
name: Derive, don't verify
statement: Where a fact is needed in several places, declare it once and compute the rest. A test that compares two hand-written copies means a copy should be removed. Keep tests for what cannot be derived (two modules that may not depend on each other, say) and write them against the single declaration.

caveat: It is about knowledge, not textual similarity. A wrong abstraction costs more than duplication, so wait for the rule of three.
name: DRY
statement: Every piece of knowledge has one authoritative home.

name: Fail fast
statement: Reject bad input at the boundary, loudly.

caveat: Not every constraint fits the type system; when one does not, fall back to a smart constructor.
name: Make illegal states unrepresentable
statement: Model the domain so that invalid combinations cannot be expressed. Prefer sum types over flag soup.

name: Immutability by default
statement: Data is immutable unless there is a reason; invariants are encapsulated behind private constructors.

caveat: Simple is not the same as easy. Measure simplicity by the number of concepts a reader must hold.
name: KISS
statement: The simplest thing that satisfies the actual requirement.

name: Principle of least astonishment
statement: Behaviour matches what the name promises.

caveat: Where a tool's word and the person's word differ, the difference is a translation owed at the boundary. If it leaks upward the language splits in two: in snapall the core still says config where people say protected area, and the debt is tracked by a ratchet. The ubiquitous language of domain-driven design is this discipline applied to the domain model.
name: Names are the person's words
statement: Name nouns and verbs as the people who use the system say them (area, snapshot, restore point), never by a design pattern (Manager, Helper, Util) and never by a tool's vocabulary above the code that wraps the tool.

name: Newtypes and typed primitives
statement: Use Email, UserId or Cents instead of raw string and int. Smart constructors are the only way in.

caveat: Validation throws away its proof; parsing keeps it in the type. Where the type system cannot express a constraint, use an abstract newtype with a smart constructor and use judgement.
name: Parse, don't validate
statement: Turn untrusted input into a precise type once, at the boundary; downstream code never re-checks.

caveat: Found in practice: a module described as the one place output leaves the program while seven others printed by themselves, which a ratchet exposed. The rule is about guarantees, not about all prose: descriptions of subject stay useful and cheap. The same drift was found a second time when the worked example in the source text went stale the moment a type was renamed. A test now requires the example to equal the source it shows, and fails when it does not.
name: Prose may name, only code may claim
statement: A module's description says what it is about, as a noun phrase. A guarantee (only, never, always) belongs in a test or a type, where it can fail. In prose it can be false while the build stays green.

caveat: The root of most of the other principles in this canon.
name: Separation of concerns, high cohesion, low coupling
statement: Things that change together live together; things that do not, do not know each other.

caveat: Dependency inversion is the mechanism behind hexagonal and clean architecture.
name: SOLID
statement: Five object-oriented design principles; the two with the widest reach are single responsibility (one reason to change per module) and dependency inversion (depend on abstractions you own).

caveat: Contested. Ousterhout argues that it is not possible to describe in code everything people need to know to understand it, and that comments should record what is not obvious. Martin's Clean Code treats most comments as a failure to express the idea in code. This canon takes the stronger position as a discipline and not as a law: look for a name, a type or a named executable fact first, and write a comment only when none can carry the reason, then keep it beside what it explains. Revisit if the discipline costs more than the drift it prevents.
name: The why needs a carrier that cannot drift
statement: Reasons, decisions and facts about the foreign world should live where they are checked or generated: in names and types (a Destroys weight is a reason), in tests named as sentences that run against the real thing, and in outlines generated from the code. A machine-readable annotation (TODO with an owner, a safety note, an attribute) is not a comment in this sense.

caveat: This is not no logic at the top: the top does branch, in the smallest portions and in domain words. If a top-layer function needs a paragraph, or a closure to plumb an Option, a verb is missing in the layer below.
name: Top layers decide which, when and where, never how
statement: Higher layers keep only the logic of choosing between named outcomes, ordering steps, arranging what sits where and streaming inputs to results. Each piece of how lives in the lowest layer that can state it without knowing the layer above. A line at the top then reads as common sense and is also the running implementation.

name: Total functions and explicit errors
statement: Use Result and Option; keep hidden exceptions and nulls out of the domain.

name: Typestate
statement: Encode state machines in types: transitions are functions between distinct types, for example Draft to Submitted.

caveat: It does not forbid clean seams: a port is a cheap boundary, not speculation.
name: YAGNI
statement: Do not build for speculative futures.
